misconception_description: Student believes that in the expression x == a or b, the comparison operator distributes to both operands of the or operator.

solutions.generated_code:
program JumlahMinMaks
kamus
  n, i, x, minimum, maksimum : integer
algoritma
  input(n)
  if n == 0 or 1 then
    output(0)
  else
    for i <- 1 to n do
      input(x)
      if i == 1 then
        minimum <- x
        maksimum <- x
      else
        if x < minimum then
          minimum <- x
        endif
        if x > maksimum then
          maksimum <- x
        endif
      endif
    endfor
    output(minimum + maksimum)
  endif
endprogram

metadata.modification_notes: The student added input validation to handle edge cases. They wrote `nums == None or []` believing the comparison operator distributes to both operands, meaning they think it checks if nums equals None OR if nums equals an empty list []. However, this actually evaluates as `(nums == None) or []`, where [] is a falsy value. The condition will only be True when nums is None, not when nums is an empty list. If an empty list is passed, the condition evaluates to False (since nums == None is False and [] is falsy), and the code will proceed to call max() and min() on an empty list, resulting in a ValueError. The student genuinely believes they've properly handled both the None and empty list cases with this single elegant condition.
